raw:
You go back upstairs, shut the room door, and switch on the desk lamp. Its small circle of light settles over the pages in front of you while Harbour Street dims beyond the window.

For a while, the building carries on around you. Water runs in the kitchen below. A chair scrapes across the foyer floor. From the auditorium comes the occasional muffled thud of a programme board being shifted carefully, followed by Rosa’s camera shutter.

Near the end of the twenty minutes, footsteps cross the landing outside. A man’s voice—Martin’s, by its roughness—travels up from the stairs with a phrase about “the blue one,” then fades again. Downstairs, the auditorium doors open and close; the booked session appears to be ending.

When you look up from your reading, the harbour has become a scatter of lights beyond the glass, and the cinema is quieter than it was at supper.
